messages.subject: Re: Is this active?
messages.body_plain:
Ha! That's indeed not very impressive. Although it was a very visual demonstration of being able to run an R interpreter in GAE, it was also a toy example which we haven't maintained in years and it looks like something finally broke it! We'll see if we can fix that, but it is certainly not a priority for us.

Running a CLI in a browser window is not a typical use-case for Renjin. In most cases, you will want to have Renjin inside your web application, ready to calculate something that is expressed in the R programming language. Have a look at https://github.com/bedatadriven/renjin-examples/tree/master/appengine-servlet to get a web app running with just a few commands on a local instance of the GAE SDK.

Maarten-Jan

messages.subject: Using renjin as a sandbox
messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,
We are considering using renjin for running R scripts through Java, and i'm trying to understand whether i can control the following use cases:
1. stop infinite loops?
2. prevent renjin from reading/deleting files?

Basically, our requirement is to use renjin as a sandbox so it won't harm our application that wraps it.

Will appreciate your quick help,
Thanks in advance
--

messages.subject: Re: Using renjin as a sandbox
messages.body_plain:
Hi Shahar,
Sandboxing is one of the use cases around which Renjin was designed. Running untrusted code is always a challenge, and the right solution will depend on the sort of things you want R code to be able to do, but here are some pointers:
1. Provide your own FileSystemManager to control or prohibit access to the physical fs. See [1] for an example.

2. Evaluate scripts in a seperate thread with a timeout to prevent infinite loops.
3. Use SecurityManager or a library like java-sandbox [2] to prevent R code from doing nasty things like import(java.lang.System)$exit()

H

[1]https://github.com/bedatadriven/renjin/blob/master/appengine/src/main/java/org/renjin/appengine/AppEngineContextFactory.java

[2]http://blog.datenwerke.net/p/the-java-sandbox.html

HTH,
Alex

messages.subject_clean: Help: Time data from Java in Renjin
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alex,

There could a bug for the function: as.POSIXct(timeInMillis/1000, origin="1970-01-01")

When I use it, I always get an error, for example:
"org.joda.time.IllegalFieldValueException: Value -2147483648 for hourOfDay must be in the range [0,23]"

But thank you that with $time I can get that milliseconds!

On Thu, Apr 30, 2015 at 12:00 PM, Charles Zhang <c...@magick.nu> wrote:
> Hi Alex,
>
> I get you. You mean I should use a method like .getTime() in Java to import the time data object right?
>
> But the issue is, in R, I currently cannot find a method to successfully read the Java time object. And $time is not a method in R. By "$" in R, it just means to get one column from a dataframe or matrix.
>
> On Thu, Apr 30, 2015 at 11:13 AM, Bertram, Alexander <al...@bedatadriven.com> wrote:
> > Right, so if you were in Java land, you would write:
> >
> > long timeInMillis = trades.get(2).getOrderOpenTime().getTime()
> >
> > which gives you a unix timestamp: the number of milliseconds since Jan 1 1970
> >
> > Renjin understands 'long' values, it doesn't (currently) understand anything specific about java.util.Date objects, other than the fact that's a java object with properties.
> >
> > So you can write in R:
> >
> > timeInMillis <- trades[[2]]$orderOpenTime$time
> >
> > This in turn is value you can convert to an R date object using the expression
> >
> >  as.POSIXct(timeInMillis/1000, origin="1970-01-01")
> >
> > Does that make sense?
> >
> > Best,
> > Alex
> >
> > On Wed, Apr 29, 2015 at 10:35 AM, Charles Zhang <c...@magick.nu> wrote:
> > > It returns a Date (java.util.Date).
> > >
> > > On Fri, Apr 24, 2015 at 6:00 PM, Bertram, Alexander <al...@bedatadriven.com> wrote:
> > > > What type does TradeOrderUtils.parseDateString() return ?
> > > >
> > > > On Fri, Apr 24, 2015 at 5:54 PM, Charles Zhang <c...@magick.nu> wrote:
> > > > > I am not familiar with Java.
> > > > >
> > > > > The data was created like this:

> > > > > to1.setOrderCloseTime(TradeOrderUtils.parseDateString("2015-02-17T09:08:57Z"));
> > > > >
> > > > > On Fri, Apr 24, 2015 at 5:49 PM, Bertram, Alexander <al...@bedatadriven.com> wrote:
> > > > > > What is the Java class of the orderOpenTime property?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Fri, Apr 24, 2015 at 5:05 PM, Charles Zhang <c...@magick.nu> wrote:
> > > > > > > Hi Bertram,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Thanks for your reply.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > "trades" is a JSON list, where I want to get the data from and to Renjin. "orderOpenTime" is one property in "trades", and that is the time data I want to get.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I also tried your code with "$time", but failed again. I guess by "$time" you mean the column or property in JSON object? Then it should be "trades[[2]]$orderOpenTime".
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Fri, Apr 24, 2015 at 4:34 PM, Bertram, Alexander <al...@bedatadriven.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > Hi Charles,
> > > > > > > > It looks like orderOpenTime is a Java object? The error message is basically saying: "I don't know how to divide a Java object (externalptr) by a double-precision floating point number".
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > java.util.Date has a getTime() method which returns the time as the number of milliseconds since the epoch:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > trades[[2]]$orderOpenTime$time
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > should invoke this method and return a normal R number value
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > So your expression should be:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >  as.POSIXct(trades[[2]]$orderOpenTime$time/1000, origin="1970-01-01")
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > HTH,
> > > > > > > > Alex
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Fri, Apr 24, 2015 at 11:26 AM, Charles Zhang <c...@magick.nu> wrote:

> > > > > > > > > Thanks for your reply.
